title: {{NAME}} and the Fairy Cup Hidden in the Wildflower Hills
moral: The best victories are the ones where everyone who played walks away knowing they gave their best.

pages.content:
The Wildflower Hills Tournament was the strangest competition {{NAME}} had ever entered, and that was before discovering that half the opposing teams were fairies.

The pitch was a natural meadow clearing, its grass kept short by generations of grazing deer who apparently also attended matches and were discerning fans. The goals were fashioned from intertwined hawthorn branches, their crossbars looped with climbing roses. The Fairy Cup itself, around which the whole event revolved, sat on a velvet cushion at the tournament official's table: a trophy no bigger than a milk bottle, made of woven moonflower stems and a single captured dewdrop held in a cage of silver wire.

Princess Isadora, who had organised the tournament for the fifth consecutive year, moved through the competing teams with a clipboard and an expression of brisk competence, her crown pushed to one side in the way of crowns on people who are too busy to adjust them. She had founded the tournament to give the fairy teams a proper competition structure, since fairies were frequently left out of larger leagues on the grounds that their skill was impossible to measure with standard equipment.

{{NAME}}'s team, the Hill Rovers, was four young people and a fairy named Wren who had asked to join last season and was, objectively, the best player on the pitch at any given moment. Wren was four inches tall, moved at the approximate speed of a thrown dart, and read the game three moves ahead. The problem was that when she sprinted, she was literally invisible to the opposing team, which the referee had ruled was legal but was, on reflection, possibly a design flaw.

pages.content:
The semi-final against the Dusk Wings was the match {{NAME}} would remember longest.

The Dusk Wings were an all-fairy team of eight, their wings the deep amber and violet of late evening, their game a style that could only be described as weather. They moved in patterns too fast for the eye to fully process, the ball seeming to teleport between them in chains of touches so short and quick they blurred together. The meadow crowd, which included approximately four hundred fairies roosting in the hawthorn hedges, responded to every move with a sound like rain on a still lake.

{{NAME}} made the tactical adjustment at half time, crouching at the goalmouth with the team gathered around in a tight circle while Wren hovered at head height and translated the Dusk Wings' movement language into something the rest of the team could work with. She had played against them before. She knew their patterns.

'They always pass back before they pass forward,' Wren said, her voice like a small bell finding its note. 'They've been doing it their whole lives. It's habit. When the ball goes back, you already move to where it's going forward.' It was the simplest and most useful thing anyone had said all season. {{NAME}}'s eyebrows climbed. Isadora, watching from the touchline, allowed herself a small satisfied nod.

pages.content:
The second half of the semi-final was the finest passage of play anyone in the hawthorn hedges had seen in five tournaments.

Wren's read was perfectly right. Every time the Dusk Wings pulled back, {{NAME}} and the team were already repositioned for the forward pass before it came. The meadow crowd's rain-on-still-lake sound changed to something more complex, the sound of an audience encountering a surprise, repeated several times in quick succession.

Wren scored twice, both goals invisible to the referee who simply saw the ball move and made a reasonable assumption. {{NAME}} scored once with a long-range shot that curved in the way of shots struck with full conviction and more than a little luck, the ball clipping the inside of the hawthorn post and rebounding off a particularly thick cluster of climbing roses into the net. Three-one at full time.

The Dusk Wings captain, a fairy named Ember whose wings were the colour of the last second before a fire goes out, flew to {{NAME}} at the final whistle and extended a hand no bigger than a grape. 'You read us,' she said, in a voice that was impressed and gracious. 'Not many teams read us.' {{NAME}} gestured to Wren, who was performing an aerial celebration that involved three backflips and a forward roll. 'She read you,' {{NAME}} said honestly. Ember looked at Wren and then back at {{NAME}}. 'You listened to her,' Ember said. 'That's different. And rarer.'

pages.content:
The final was against Princess Isadora's own team, which created a diplomatic situation she handled by immediately recusing herself from officiating and appointing Ember as substitute referee, which everyone agreed was an inspired solution.

Isadora, it turned out, played a different game from what she administered. She was aggressive and joyful in equal measure, her crown removed and placed carefully on the touchline, her gown hitched up at the knees, her boots sensible and scuffed. She was also very good. Better than good. She was the kind of player who seemed to create extra time in the game by always being in the right place.

With five minutes to go, the score was two-all. The meadow crowd had grown to include a delegation of owls who had arrived from the night hills and stationed themselves along the upper hawthorn branches, observing with solemn attention. The light had turned to that particular burnished gold that arrives just before the day concedes to evening.

Isadora and {{NAME}} arrived at the ball at exactly the same moment, both committed, both expecting to win the challenge. They looked at each other for one suspended second. Then Isadora stepped aside and let {{NAME}} take it. Not from weakness. From the kind of generosity that only comes from genuine confidence. {{NAME}} took three touches, drew two defenders, and returned the ball to Wren, who scored from an angle mathematically determined to be impossible.

pages.content:
The Hill Rovers won three-two, and the Fairy Cup was presented by Ember with considerable ceremony and a speech that was brief because she was four inches tall and everyone had to lean in to hear.

Isadora accepted the result with the specific grace of someone who ran the thing and still competed properly, which was the hardest balance to strike and she made it look easy. She and {{NAME}} sat on the cool grass afterward with their boots off and their feet in the meadow, which was the most comfortable anyone could possibly be.

Wren had fallen asleep inside the Fairy Cup. Not in a disrespectful way. In the way of someone very small who has worked very hard and found the most perfect, exact-right-sized space to recover in.

'Next year,' Isadora said, 'I'm going to enter and not organise.' She said it the way people say things they have decided. 'Then who organises it?' {{NAME}} asked. Isadora smiled with the particular satisfaction of someone who has already worked this out. 'Ember's been asking for three years.'

{{NAME}} lay back in the meadow grass and watched the first stars find their places overhead, the Fairy Cup balanced carefully on a flat stone nearby with Wren sleeping inside it like a very small, very contented seed. Sleep now, champion. Let the meadow hold you. And wonder, in the warm dark, what Wren dreams of in a trophy made of moonflowers and silver wire.
